desc:
Document and message classification by category sorts invoices, contracts, emails and enquiries into the groups you define. Ecom Swift LLC builds the sorter, tests it on your real examples and routes each item to the right folder, label or person.

## What is document and message classification?

Classification means assigning every incoming item to one category from a list you control, such as invoice, quote request, complaint or contract. The sorter reads the content, picks the best match and then acts: it applies a label, moves the file, or hands the item to the right team. If it cannot decide with enough confidence, the item goes to a review pile instead of being forced into a wrong category.

It is the step that happens before anyone can act. Until a pile of mixed mail has been sorted, nobody knows what is urgent.

## What goes wrong when sorting is done by hand

In many small businesses one person opens the shared inbox each morning and decides where everything goes. That person becomes a bottleneck, and when they are away the pile grows. Urgent messages sit beside newsletters. Invoices get filed under general mail. A customer complaint waits two days because it looked like any other email.

Manual sorting is also inconsistent. Two people will label the same message differently, so later searches miss things and counts of enquiries by type cannot be trusted.

## How sorting changes response time and reporting

When items are sorted on arrival, each one reaches the person who can deal with it. Finance sees invoices, support sees problems, sales sees new requests. Nobody scans a mixed list to find their own work.

A sorted flow also produces clean counts. If you know how many quote requests, returns and supplier messages arrive each week, you can plan staffing and spot changes early. Priority tags add another layer, so urgent items rise above routine ones. The result depends on how clear your categories are and how consistent the incoming material is, which is why we test on your own examples first.

## What a good sorter includes

- A short, clear category list with a plain definition and a few examples for each.
- A rule for items that fit two categories, so the choice is predictable.
- Labels or folders applied automatically in the inbox or file store you already use.
- Routing to a named person, shared inbox or chat channel for each category.
- A confidence threshold, with unsure items sent to a review pile.
- Handling of both the message text and its attached files.
- Optional subcategories and priority tags, such as urgent and routine.
- A count of items by category over time.
- A simple way to add or rename a category later.

## How we set it up

We begin with a workshop-style review of your material. You send examples of each kind of item, and we propose categories, definitions and edge-case rules. You approve the list before anything is built, because the categories are the most important decision in the whole project.

Then we build the sorter, connect it to your source, and run it on your examples without touching live mail. We compare its choices with yours, look at every miss and refine the definitions. When the results are acceptable, we switch on labels, folders or routing. The Basic package covers a small category list and one source. Standard adds routing, a second source and a review pile. Premium adds subcategories, priority tags, up to three sources and a weekly count, along with a guide for adding categories yourself.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Keep categories few and distinct, and define each in one sentence.
- Give us real examples, including awkward ones that are hard to place.
- Decide who looks at the review pile and how often.
- Add a category only when a pattern of items truly needs it.
- Check a small sample of sorted items every week at first.

**Avoid:**
- Creating a category called "other" that quietly grows into the biggest group.
- Using overlapping categories that even your own team would argue about.
- Sending every sorted item straight to an automatic reply before you trust the sorting.
- Sorting by sender name alone, since senders write about many topics.
- Ignoring the review pile, which defeats the purpose of flagging unsure items.

## Who this service is for

It suits a small agency whose shared inbox mixes client requests with invoices and spam-like offers. It suits an operations manager who receives scanned paperwork in one folder and needs it split by type before filing. It also suits a business with a backlog of old mail that must be organized once, then kept in order from now on.

## What we need from you

Please send a spread of examples, ideally fifty or more across your main item types, with the category you would give each. Tell us where items arrive and where they should end up. We never ask for passwords. Access is given as a collaborator, team user or delegated mailbox user, depending on the tool, and everything is built in your own accounts.
